questions.q: According to the lesson, what typically makes up the largest part of an AI application's actual dependency footprint?
options: The team's own application code
A pretrained model, third-party datasets, and open-source orchestration packages, not the team's own code
The company's marketing website
The user's own device hardware
questions.explain: The lesson states the team's own code is usually the smallest part, with pretrained models, datasets, and packages making up the rest.

questions.q: What is a 'backdoored' or poisoned model, as described in the lesson?
options: A model that has been fine-tuned to include a hidden trigger behavior, behaving normally except when it sees a specific phrase
A model that runs slower than average
A model that requires a password to download
A model that has been deleted from a public hub
questions.explain: The lesson describes a poisoned model as one with a hidden trigger behavior fine-tuned in, looking like a normal release otherwise.

questions.q: What is 'dataset poisoning' per the lesson?
options: Deleting a dataset entirely
Encrypting a dataset so it can't be used
Mixing a small number of subtly crafted or mislabeled examples into an otherwise legitimate-looking training dataset to implant unwanted behavior
Compressing a dataset to save storage space
questions.explain: The lesson defines dataset poisoning as crafted examples mixed into training data that implant unwanted behavior without being obvious on casual inspection.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say supply chain risk is easy for builders to overlook?
options: Because it never actually causes any real problems
Because downloading a model or installing a package feels like routine development, not like accepting an unreviewed third-party binary into production
Because only large companies are affected by it
Because it is clearly labeled as dangerous by every package registry
questions.explain: The lesson highlights the mismatch between how routine these actions feel and how much trust they actually grant, which is what makes the risk easy to skip past.

questions.q: What does the lesson recommend regarding dependency versions for an AI stack?
options: Pin dependency versions with a lockfile rather than always pulling the latest version
Always use the newest available version of every package automatically
Avoid using any open-source packages at all
Dependency versioning doesn't matter for AI projects
questions.explain: The lesson's checklist recommends pinning versions and using a lockfile, rather than always pulling latest, as part of managing supply chain risk.
